name: Crocodile breathing
description: Diaphragmatic breathing in prone position to set parasympathetic tone for the morning routine.
setup: Lie face down on the floor, forehead resting on stacked hands
Feet hip width, toes pointed straight back
Inhale into the belly so it presses into the floor and pushes the lower back up toward the ceiling
Exhale slow through the nose, feel the belly soften
cues: Feel the breath in the back and sides of the torso, not the chest
Slow exhale is the key — twice as long as inhale if possible
This is the relax primer: let global muscle tension go before the holds — set a loose baseline so the day isn't one long brace

name: Glute bridge iso
description: Wakes the glutes before any standing work. Foundational position that makes everything downstream organize correctly.
setup: Lie on back, knees bent, feet flat on floor hip width
Position feet so when bridged, shins are vertical (heels close to glutes)
Drive through heels, lift hips until knees-hips-shoulders form a straight line
Squeeze glutes hard, ribs stay down, no arching the lower back
cues: If you feel it in hamstrings or lower back, walk feet slightly farther out
Should feel primarily in the glutes

name: Short foot activation
description: Foot-to-floor connection. Trains the arch to support actively from below.
setup: Stand barefoot, feet hip width
Spread toes wide, then press ball of foot and heel into the floor while drawing them toward each other
The arch should lift
Keep toes long and flat, do not curl them
Hold the foot in this active position, feel the arch supporting from below
cues: Toes long, not curled
Arch lifts because of pressure between ball and heel, not because you flex

name: Spanish squat iso
description: Patella tendon health and quad endurance in a controlled position. The band counterbalances and protects the knees.
setup: Anchor a band around a sturdy post at hip height
Loop the band behind your knees, step back so the band is taut and pulling your knees forward
Squat down to ~90 degrees; the band counterbalances and allows shins to stay vertical
Hold the bottom position, chest up, knees tracking over toes
cues: Controlled patella tendon loading with shins vertical
The position the tendon needs to adapt to for landing absorption
If band feels insufficient, sub a wall sit at 90 degrees temporarily
Brace only the working muscles — don't globally clench; relax-fire: hold with intent, then FULLY release between sets, no carried-over tension

name: Single-leg RDL hold
description: Posterior chain loading single-leg. Glute already awake from glute bridge so this engages hamstring and glute cleanly.
setup: Stand on one leg, soft knee in standing leg
Hinge at the hip while the free leg extends straight back behind you
Stop when the torso and free leg are parallel to the floor (T-shape)
Reaching arms forward for counterbalance is fine
Hold. Feel hamstring of standing leg lengthening under tension, glute engaged
cues: Left leg first, every day
Free leg straight, no bend at the knee
Hips square to the floor, do not let the free-leg hip rise

name: Split squat iso
description: Specifically rehearses the dunk-relevant loaded position. Front leg is doing the work.
setup: Take a long step forward into split stance
Drop straight down until back knee hovers just above the floor
Front shin should be vertical, weight in the heel and mid-foot of the front leg
Torso upright, ribs stacked, no lean forward
cues: Front glute should burn hard
If front quad is dominant, shift slightly more weight to the heel
Left leg as the front leg first
Relax-fire: hold with intent, then fully release between sets — don't carry a constant brace

name: Active squat hold at parallel
description: NOT a passive rock-bottom hold. Depth is femur-parallel where muscles actively produce force, not where joint capsule absorbs tissue stretch.
setup: Feet shoulder width or slightly wider, toes turned out very slightly
Descend slowly into a squat where the femur is roughly parallel to the floor
Chest up, arms extended forward for counterbalance or holding a doorframe lightly for support
Active position: gently push knees out, drive chest up, create tension throughout
cues: Quads and glutes should be BURNING (muscles actively producing force)
Should NOT feel knee tendons being passively stretched
If tendon stretch, come up an inch or two until burn is in the muscles
Why not ass-to-grass: with patella tendon history, rock-bottom puts load on connective tissue rather than producing real isometric work

name: Extreme push-up hold
description: Upper-body extreme isometric: hold a mid/low push-up position and actively pull yourself deeper with maximal intent.
setup: Push-up position, lower to mid-range (elbows about 90 degrees)
Hold, actively pulling the chest toward the floor and the floor toward you
Brace the whole body: glutes, abs, quads tight
Build the hold time over weeks before adding difficulty
cues: If you aren't pulling, you're fooling - contract, don't just hang there
Whole body rigid, no sagging hips
Breathe shallow and keep the tension

name: Scapular hang (active/passive)
description: Hang from a bar, alternating an active shoulder-down hang with a relaxed passive hang. Builds shoulder isometric capacity and decompresses.
setup: Hang from a bar, arms straight
Active phase: pull the shoulder blades down and together, away from the ears
Passive phase: relax briefly, then re-engage
Build total hang time over weeks
cues: Active: pull the shoulders down, ribs down
Stay engaged with intent, breathe
Grip and shoulders both working

name: Overhead wall iso press
description: Press the hands up into a locked overhead position against a wall/frame and hold with maximal intent. The overhead-pattern extreme isometric.
setup: Stand tall, press the hands overhead into a wall or door frame
Ribs down, glutes tight, push up hard the whole time
Pull into the position - biceps by the ears, full overhead reach
Build the hold time over weeks
cues: Push up hard continuously - pull into the position, do not relax
Ribs down, do not arch the lower back
Full overhead position, arms by the ears

name: Calf iso, plantarflexion, bent knee
description: Soleus and Achilles, single leg, bent knee biases the workhorse muscle for running and jumping support.
setup: Stand on one leg, bend the standing knee slightly (15 to 20 degrees)
Raise up onto the ball of the foot as high as possible
Hold the top position, weight directly over the ball of the foot
cues: Bent knee takes the gastrocnemius out and isolates the soleus
Soleus is the muscle that absorbs and produces force during running and the loading phase of a jump
Left leg first

name: Tibialis raises
description: Counterbalance to the calf work. Trains the front of the shin, critical for ankle health and shin splint prevention.
setup: Stand with heels against a wall, toes pointed forward
Lift the toes and forefoot as high as possible toward the shin
Hold the top for a beat, lower slowly
cues: Iso version: simply hold the top position rather than doing reps
Either version works

name: Open-chain terminal knee-extension iso (VMO lock)
description: The safe version of the 'lock' that bothered you on the machine — isometric only, no loaded lowering. Drives the quad/VMO to seat the kneecap and hold the knee straight in open chain.
setup: Long-sit with the working leg straight, a rolled towel under the knee
Pull the toes toward you and drive the knee straight down into the towel
Squeeze the quad as hard as you can so the kneecap pulls up and the knee locks
Hold the lock; breathe; keep the contraction strong the whole time
Relax fully between holds — never lower under load through range
cues: Isometric ONLY — this is the part that felt fine; the loaded lowering is what we're avoiding
Chase a hard kneecap glide, especially on the left
No leg-extension machine, no ankle weight
Keep it pain-free and out of any range that feels unstable

name: Hip flexor stretch with active contraction
description: Opens the hip flexor and actively reinforces glute engagement so the new pattern carries into the day.
setup: Half-kneeling lunge position, back knee on a pad
Tuck the pelvis (squeeze the back glute hard, pull the pubic bone toward the belly button)
Front foot flat, front shin vertical
You should feel a strong stretch in the front of the back hip
cues: Active back-glute squeeze is the key
Passive stretching does much less than this
The contraction is what reinforces the pattern

name: Tactile feedback step-down
description: Biofeedback drill. Hand on the front of the left quad — the quad must stay soft on the landing while the glute and hamstring absorb.
setup: Stand on top of a 4 to 6 inch box (a step, a low platform)
Left leg planted on the box, right leg hanging off the side
Place your right hand flat on the front of the left quad
Slowly bend the left knee and lower the right heel toward the floor
Stop the instant the right heel touches the floor. Do not transfer weight.
Return to the start position, slowly
cues: Left quad should stay soft under your hand throughout
If it tenses hard, you are using the wrong pattern — stop, reset, slow down
What should fire: left glute and left hamstring (as the brake)

name: Wall-supported single-leg squat
description: Wall removes balance demand so the nervous system focuses on glute-hamstring sequencing without quad rescue.
setup: Stand with back flat against a wall, feet roughly 12 inches out from the wall
Shift weight to the left leg, lift the right leg straight out in front
Slide down the wall slowly (5 second descent) until left thigh is roughly parallel to the floor
Hold the bottom position for 2 seconds
Press back up to standing through the left heel
cues: Wall takes balance out of the equation
The work is pure single-leg posterior chain loading on the left
If 90 degrees is too deep, go to 60 degrees and progress depth over time

name: Eccentric single-leg sit-to-stand from high box
description: Builds eccentric capacity in the left leg. The slow descent is the rewiring stimulus; stand up uses both legs.
setup: Set up in front of a box or bench roughly knee height (a standard 18 inch bench works)
Stand on the left leg, right leg held off the ground in front
Slowly sit back and down onto the box, taking 5 full seconds for the descent
Let your butt fully touch the box
Stand up using BOTH legs (this is intentional, the descent is the work)
cues: Concentric work on a single leg this early can recruit the wrong pattern
The slow eccentric is the rewiring stimulus
Five-second descent, full butt-to-box, two-leg stand

name: Single-leg deadlift with light DB
description: Motor learning, not strength work. Posterior chain takes the load the quad has been hijacking.
setup: Hold a 15 to 25 lb DB in the right hand (opposite hand to the standing leg)
Stand on the left leg, soft knee
Hinge at the hip slowly, taking 5 full seconds to descend
Free leg extends straight back behind you, the DB lowers toward the floor in front
Stop at the parallel position (torso parallel to floor)
Hold the bottom for 2 seconds
Stand back up over 3 seconds, driving through the left heel and squeezing the left glute
cues: DB is light on purpose — this is motor learning, not strength work
Load comes after the pattern is bulletproof, not before
5 sec eccentric, 2 sec hold, 3 sec concentric

name: Quad set + straight-leg raise (open chain)
description: The most direct tool for the residual quad/VMO inhibition (AMI) — teaches the quad to fire and seat the kneecap with the foot free, no joint compression to lean on. No machine, no ankle weight.
setup: Long-sit or lie on your back, the working leg straight, a rolled towel under the knee
Set the quad FIRST: drive the knee down into the towel and squeeze hard so the kneecap glides up and the knee locks straight
Holding that lock, raise the whole straight leg a few inches (foot stays pulled toward you)
Lower slowly under control, keeping the quad switched on the whole way
Reset and repeat; give the inhibited (left) side extra focus
cues: The quad set is the point — no kneecap glide, no rep
Keep the knee dead straight; never let it bend and re-straighten under the lift
Open chain on purpose — NO leg-extension machine and no ankle weight yet
Stay out of any range where the knee feels like it could shift

name: Open-chain knee position sense
description: Trains joint-position sense in open chain — the proprioceptive map a subluxation feeling often reflects. Seated, leg free, learn to find and reproduce a knee angle without looking.
setup: Sit tall on a chair or box, working leg hanging free
Slowly straighten the knee to a target angle, pause and memorize how it feels
Close your eyes, let the leg relax down, then reproduce the same angle
Open your eyes and check; adjust and repeat at a few different angles
Work only through ranges that feel stable
cues: Slow and deliberate — this is sensing, not strengthening
Quality of the match matters more than the rep count
Avoid any angle where the knee feels like it shifts
Keep the quad gently active throughout

name: Banded rhythmic stabilization (open chain)
description: Reflexive joint-centering: small, fast perturbations to the free leg train the quad and hamstring to co-contract and hold the knee centered without ground feedback. The Marinovich rapid-response idea applied open chain.
setup: Sit tall, working leg extended to a stable mid-range angle, band looped around the shin and anchored to the side
Hold the leg still against the band's pull
Give the leg small, fast oscillating pulses (or have the band tugged from different directions) and resist — keep the knee from drifting
Work in short bursts, keeping the joint quiet and centered
Switch the anchor side to challenge different directions
cues: Small and fast — co-contract, don't let the knee wobble
Stay in a stable mid-range; no end-range or unstable angles
~15-20 sec of pulses per set
Stop if the knee feels like it could shift

name: Dynamic rotating bridge on the ball
description: The connection drill — teaches the legs to anchor and drive while the hips and core rotate and transfer force, so the lower body stops working as a locked block. Closed-chain (feet planted) and low-impact: the whole-body rotation work done on the ball, programmed controlled-first.
setup: Rest your upper back and shoulders on the ball, hips lifted into a tabletop bridge, feet flat hip-width, knees about 90 degrees
Keep the hips up and level, glutes engaged
Slowly rotate the torso so your shoulders roll across the ball to one side, then the other
Drive through the feet and let the legs and hips steer the roll — the legs anchor, the hips transfer the rotation
Start slow and fully controlled; add speed only as control (and the knee) allow
cues: Legs drive into the floor and steer the rotation — not the arms or shoulders
Stay loose between moves: relax, then move — no global clenching
Hips stay up and level; don't let one side dip
Progress over weeks: slow and owned -> faster -> reactive
Knees track over the toes; back off if the left knee feels unstable

name: Supine adductor squeeze pulses
description: Rapid adductor (inner-thigh) firing — speed of firing, not force. The 55 cm ball is too big to kick between the knees, so this trains the same fast inner-thigh firing as light squeeze-pulses with the ball trapped so it can't roll.
setup: Lie on your back, knees bent about 90 degrees, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart
Set the 55 cm ball between your knees — it is too big to fit deep between them, so just rest the inside of each knee against its sides
Press both knees gently inward so the ball is lightly trapped and cannot roll away
From that light contact, squeeze in and release rapidly — fast, small, light pulses with the inner thighs (quick on-off-on-off, not a hard crush)
Keep your back, hips, and shoulders relaxed on the floor; only the inner thighs are working
cues: Speed of firing, not force — switch the inner thighs on and off fast, do not grind the ball
Should feel rhythmic and light; breathing stays easy and relaxed
If your core is bracing hard or you are holding your breath, you are using too much force — lighten up and speed up
Lower back and glutes stay relaxed — this is all inner thigh

name: Supine alternating ball taps (toes)
description: Rapid alternating hip flexor firing. Very fast, very light — the taps are barely contacting the ball.
setup: Lie on your back on the floor
Place the 55 cm ball about a foot or two beyond your feet
Lift both legs up so the toes are roughly above the top of the ball
Begin rapidly alternating: tap the top of the ball with the toes of the left foot, then the right foot, as fast as possible
Knees stay slightly bent throughout — hip flexors do the work, not the lower back
cues: If lower back arches off the floor, hip flexors are tight or you are reaching too far
Bring the ball slightly closer to your hips for a more comfortable angle
Light, fast contacts

name: Prone alternating heel-to-glute flicks
description: Posterior-chain version of the toe taps — teaches the hamstring to fire independently of the quad (the co-contraction drill). Face-down, your heels point up, so there is nothing on the floor to tap; the target is your own glute as you flick the heel toward it.
setup: Lie face down on the floor, legs straight, forehead resting on your stacked hands
Optional: slide the 55 cm ball under your hips and lower belly so your lower back stays flat and comfortable — or lie flat if that feels fine
Quickly bend one knee to flick that heel up toward your glute, then let it drop as you flick the other heel up
Alternate left, right, left, right as fast as you can — like quick, light butt-kicks done lying down
Keep the flicks small and snappy; the heel travels toward your butt, driven by the back of the thigh
cues: Speed, not force — fast light flicks; the hamstring switches on and off while the quad stays relaxed
This is the drill most directly attacking the co-contraction problem
Keep your hips pressed into the floor — do not let your butt hike up or your lower back arch
If your lower back arches or your hip flexors cramp, slow down and make the flicks smaller

name: Seated rapid hip rotations on ball
description: Fascial slings of the trunk and hips firing in rapid alternation. Trains exactly the sequencing used in approach jumps.
setup: Sit tall on top of the 55 cm ball, feet flat on the floor about hip-width apart, weight even on both feet
Rest your hands lightly on your hips, or hold them out in front of you for balance
Keep your head and shoulders facing forward and still, as if they are fixed in place
Quickly swivel your hips and seat to the left, then to the right, letting the ball roll a few inches side to side underneath you
The movement comes from your pelvis only and stays small — a few inches each way, fast and rhythmic, not a big twist
cues: Only your hips and the ball move — shoulders and head stay square to the front
Small and fast: a quick rhythmic swivel side to side
Keep both feet planted; let the ball roll under you rather than lifting a foot
Trains the fast hip-rotation sequencing an approach jump uses to turn run-up speed into lift

name: Quadruped rocking on ball
description: Whole-body coordination drill — fascial system firing as a coordinated whole rather than as isolated muscle groups.
setup: Kneel on the floor with the 55 cm ball on the ground just in front of you
Place both hands on top of the ball, shoulder-width apart, arms roughly straight
Walk your knees back a little and lean your weight onto the ball, so you are on your hands and knees with the ball under your hands
Rock your whole body forward a few inches — weight shifts onto your hands and the ball rolls slightly forward — then rock back to the start
Keep it small and continuous: quick little rocks forward and back, hands staying on top of the ball the whole time
cues: Move as one piece — small fast adjustments through your whole body, not just bending your arms
Keep a flat back and a gently braced middle; do not let your lower back sag
Small range — the ball only rolls a few inches each way
This one is steady coordination, not max speed; the bout is a bit longer (20 sec) for that reason

name: Smith machine squat
description: Primary lower-body strength. Heavy bilateral squat, Yates-style: ramp to two all-out working sets.
setup: Bar across the upper back, feet slightly forward of the bar line

Drive the floor away to lockout
Two all-out working sets to honest failure or one rep short

description: CNS-priming loaded isometric. Post-activation potentiation before jumping work. Left forward first.

Weight in front HEEL, not ball of foot
Drop straight down: back knee descends toward floor (not backward)
Bottom position: back knee hovers an inch above floor
Torso vertical: ribs stacked over hips, no leaning forward
cues: Left leg forward first, always

Relax, then snap to the ball

Quiet, low contacts - no big steps
Short bursts, then full rest

name: Reaction start / get-up
description: React to a random cue from a ready position and explode into a 1-2 step acceleration. Trains reactive acceleration - the start of athletic quickness.

On an unpredictable cue (beep, dropped ball, a partner), explode up and forward
Accelerate hard for 1-2 steps, then reset
Vary the start position and the cue so it stays a reaction, not a routine
cues: HOLD: do not perform until the knee swelling is fully resolved
React to the stimulus - do not pre-move or anticipate
First step low and powerful, full recovery between reps
Ease in sub-maximal, build speed as the knee tolerates

name: Knee-to-wall ankle dorsiflexion
description: Weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion mobility. Reduced dorsiflexion is one of the most consistently established contributors to knee-in collapse, and it is fully non-impact to train.
setup: Face a wall in a half-kneel or split stance, front foot a few inches back from the wall
Keeping the heel flat and glued down, drive the knee forward to touch the wall directly over the middle toes
If it touches easily, slide the foot back and repeat; if the heel lifts, move closer
Move slowly in and out of end range for reps, don't bounce
cues: Knee tracks straight over the 2nd/3rd toe, not caving inward
Heel stays welded to the floor the whole time — that's what makes it real range
Work the range you own today; end range grows week to week

name: Foot tripod stance
description: Trains active control of the three-point foot base (big-toe ball, little-toe ball, heel) — the platform the whole leg organizes over.
setup: Stand barefoot, weight even
Find three points on the working foot: base of the big toe, base of the little toe, centre of the heel
Press all three lightly into the floor and lift the arch slightly without curling the toes
Hold, breathing easy, toes long and relaxed
cues: Toes long and soft — the lift comes from the arch, not from gripping
Imagine spreading the floor apart under the ball of the foot
Even pressure on all three points, especially the big-toe base

name: Toe yoga (big-toe / lesser-toe control)
description: Intrinsic foot control and toe independence. Restores the ability to load the big toe, which anchors the arch and the tripod.
setup: Stand or sit with the foot flat
Press only the big toe down while lifting the other four toes
Then reverse: keep the big toe lifted while pressing the four little toes down
Alternate slowly and deliberately for reps
cues: Slow and precise beats fast and sloppy — you're rebuilding a connection
Keep the rest of the foot quiet; isolate the toes
Frustrating at first is normal — the control comes back with practice

name: Short-foot in single-leg stance
description: Progresses the short-foot arch action into single-leg stance, where the arch must actually resist collapse under body weight — the point where foot control meets knee control.
setup: Stand on one foot, barefoot, near a wall or rail for a fingertip touch if needed
Set the short foot: press ball and heel toward each other so the arch lifts, toes long
Balance quietly, holding the active arch
Watch the knee — keep it pointing over the middle of the foot
cues: Arch stays lifted, toes stay long — no gripping or clawing
Knee tracks over the 2nd toe; if it drifts in, reset from the foot up
Quiet foot, quiet knee — control the small wobbles

name: Slow-tempo heel raise (controlled)
description: Builds calf/ankle capacity through a slow, controlled range with no impact — the eccentric lowering trains ankle stiffness the leg needs without any ground reaction spike.
setup: Stand tall, balls of the feet on a step edge, heels free, fingertip support for balance
Rise up smoothly over 2 seconds to full height
Lower over 3–4 seconds to a deep stretch below the step
No bounce at the bottom — control the turnaround
cues: Slow and smooth both directions; the lowering is the point
Push evenly through the big-toe and little-toe base, don't roll to the outside
Full range top and bottom

name: Side-lying hip abduction (control)
description: Targets gluteus medius through a clean, controlled range. The cue set turns it from a strength rep into a motor-control rep — leading with the heel and keeping the pelvis still.
setup: Lie on your side, bottom knee bent for stability, top leg straight in line with the torso
Roll the top hip very slightly forward so the kneecap points straight ahead (or heel slightly higher than toe)
Lift the top leg to about 30–40 degrees, leading with the heel
Lower slowly with control; don't let the pelvis roll back
cues: Lead with the heel, toe slightly down — that keeps it in the glute, not the hip flexor/TFL
Pelvis stays stacked and still; the leg moves, the trunk doesn't
Feel it in the side of the hip pocket, not the low back

name: Banded clamshell (pelvis-still)
description: Gluteus medius / external-rotator activation with the pelvis locked — the point is that the pelvis does NOT roll back, so the glute does the work instead of the low back.
setup: Side-lying, mini band above the knees, hips and knees bent ~45 degrees, feet together
Stack the pelvis vertical; place the top hand on the top hip to feel it stay still
Open the top knee against the band while keeping the feet together and the pelvis dead still
Lower slowly under control
cues: The pelvis must not roll backward — if it does, you're cheating with the trunk
Drive the knee open, feel the side of the glute switch on
Slow open, slow close; own the band

name: Banded lateral walk
description: A moving glute-medius pattern: hold an athletic mini-squat and step sideways against the band while keeping the knees pushed out over the toes — directly rehearsing the anti-valgus action under motion.
setup: Mini band around the legs (above knees to start, around ankles to progress)
Sink into a quarter-squat, chest up, knees pushed out so there's tension in the band
Step sideways with control, keeping constant band tension — knees never cave inward
Take the prescribed steps one way, then back the other way
cues: Knees stay pushed OUT toward the little toes the whole time — never let them drift in
Stay low and level; don't bob up and down or waddle the hips
Slow, deliberate steps — quality of the knee line is the whole exercise

name: Single-leg pelvic-level control
description: The direct anti-Trendelenburg drill: stand on one leg and keep the pelvis level, so the stance-side glute medius learns to control the hip from above — the mechanism that stops the knee-in collapse.
setup: Stand on one leg near a mirror, hands on the top of the pelvis (on the hip bones)
Level the pelvis so both hip bones sit at the same height
Hold the level pelvis; then progress by slowly dipping and re-levelling the free-side hip with control
Keep the stance knee soft and tracking over the toes
cues: Both hip bones stay level — don't let the free-side hip drop
Drive down through the stance heel and feel the side glute hold the pelvis up
Stance knee points over the 2nd toe, foot in tripod

name: Hip airplane
description: Advanced single-leg hip-control drill: a hinge with controlled internal/external rotation of the stance hip. Trains the glute to control rotation — the rotational component of dynamic valgus. Enters once single-leg control is solid.
setup: Stand on one leg, hinge forward to a flat-back position, arms out or a rail under one hand for support
From the hinged position, slowly rotate the pelvis open (free hip toward the ceiling)
Then rotate it closed (free hip toward the floor), controlling the motion with the STANCE hip
Keep the spine long and the stance knee tracking over the toes
cues: The stance hip drives the rotation, not the low back
Slow, controlled arc both directions — no wobble at the ends
Foot tripod stays set; knee never caves in as you rotate

name: Side plank (lateral chain)
description: The frontal-plane core hold. Lateral-core control is one of the trunk contributors to keeping the knee out of valgus during single-leg tasks; this trains the whole lateral chain from shoulder to hip.
setup: Lie on your side, elbow under the shoulder, forearm flat, knees bent (easier) or legs straight (harder)
Lift the hips so the body is one straight line from head to knees/feet
Squeeze the down-side glute, ribs stacked, don't let the hips sag
Hold and breathe
cues: One straight line — no hips sagging toward the floor and no piking up
Push the floor away with the forearm; stay long through the top side
Breathe steadily; brace the trunk, not the neck

name: Pallof anti-rotation press
description: Anti-rotation core. Standing and resisting a sideways pull teaches the trunk to stay stacked over the pelvis — the trunk-control half of keeping the knee stacked over the foot.
setup: Anchor a band at chest height; stand side-on, feet hip width, band held at the chest with both hands
Step out so the band is taut, pulling you toward the anchor
Press the hands straight out from the chest and hold — resist the band's pull to rotate you
Return slowly to the chest; keep the hips and shoulders square the whole time
cues: Do NOT let the band twist you — stay square to the front
Ribs down, glutes on, resist the rotation from the trunk
Slow press out, slow return; the hold at full reach is the work

name: Dead bug
description: Anti-extension core with limb dissociation — the trunk stays quiet and braced while the arms and legs move independently. Trains the coordination of keeping a stable centre while the limbs work.
setup: Lie on your back, arms reaching to the ceiling, hips and knees bent to 90 degrees
Flatten the low back gently into the floor and keep it there
Slowly lower the opposite arm and leg toward the floor, keeping the back flat
Return and switch sides, moving slowly
cues: Low back stays glued to the floor — if it arches, shorten the range
Move slowly; exhale as the limbs reach out
The trunk stays perfectly still while the arms and legs move

name: Bird dog
description: Contralateral coordination and posterior-chain control on all fours — links opposite arm and leg through a stable trunk, reinforcing the cross-body pattern used in single-leg stance.
setup: On hands and knees, hands under shoulders, knees under hips, spine long and neutral
Reach the opposite arm forward and leg back until both are level with the trunk
Keep the pelvis level — don't let it tip or rotate
Return with control and switch sides
cues: Reach long, don't hike — hips stay square to the floor
Imagine a glass of water on the low back that must not spill
Slow and controlled; pause a beat at full reach

name: Mirror single-leg mini-squat (external focus)
description: The centrepiece rewiring drill. A slow single-leg mini-squat performed watching the knee in a mirror, using an external-focus cue to keep the knee tracking over the foot. Real-time visual feedback plus external-focus cueing is the intervention with the strongest and fastest evidence for reducing knee valgus.
setup: Stand on one leg facing a mirror so you can see the knee and foot
Set the foot tripod and a level pelvis
Slowly bend the knee a few inches, watching that the kneecap stays pointing over the 2nd/3rd toe
Descend only as far as you can keep the knee tracking, then return; move slowly
cues: Watch the knee in the mirror — keep it pointing at your middle toes, never letting it dive inward
External-focus cue: 'spread the floor apart with your foot' and 'shine a headlight straight ahead with your kneecap'
Small range done perfectly beats deep range with any cave-in — depth grows as control does
Silent, smooth, controlled — no wobble, no collapse

name: Single-leg balance progression
description: Proprioception and static single-leg control. Progresses by removing feedback and adding instability — eyes open, then eyes closed, then on a cushion — so the ankle, knee and hip learn to hold alignment without conscious watching.
setup: Stand on one leg, foot in tripod, knee soft and tracking over the toes, pelvis level
Level 1: hold with eyes open near a wall for a fingertip touch if needed
Level 2 (Phase 2+): eyes closed
Level 3 (Phase 3+): stand on a cushion or folded towel, eyes open then closed
cues: Quiet foot: control the small wobbles from the arch and ankle, not by flailing the arms
Knee stays soft and over the 2nd toe; pelvis stays level
When it gets easy, take away a sense (close the eyes) or add instability (cushion)

name: Single-leg multi-directional reach
description: Dynamic single-leg control (a Y-balance / star-excursion pattern). Standing on one leg and reaching the other foot out in different directions loads the stance hip and knee through controlled range in every plane — dynamic balance with no impact.
setup: Stand on one leg, foot in tripod, hands on hips or out for balance
Reach the free foot slowly forward and tap the floor lightly, then return to standing tall
Repeat reaching to the side, then diagonally back — a slow, controlled 'star'
Keep the stance knee bending over the toes as you reach; return to full height each time
cues: The stance knee tracks over the 2nd toe on every reach — never let it cave in
Light tap, then control the return — don't fall out to the reaching foot
Stay tall through the spine; the stance leg does the controlling

name: Banded wall sit with knee-drive
description: An isometric that actively trains the anti-valgus action: hold a wall sit with a band around the knees and press the knees outward against it. Combines a quad-friendly isometric (good for swelling-related quad inhibition) with a glute-medius knee-out drive.
setup: Mini band just above the knees; sit back against a wall with thighs toward parallel, shins vertical
Feet hip-width, in tripod, knees over the middle toes
Press the knees gently OUT into the band and hold that outward tension for the whole set
Breathe easy; keep the outward knee pressure constant
cues: Knees push out against the band the entire hold — never let them drift in
Even pressure through both feet; drive through the heels and the big-toe base
Quiet, steady hold — brace the working muscles, don't clench everything; relax fully between sets

name: Mirror single-leg squats (slow tempo)
description: The daily grooving version of the rewiring drill: slow, continuous single-leg mini-squats performed watching the knee in a mirror, holding the external-focus cue. Timed rather than counted so it slots into the daily foundation — the point is frequent, low-effort exposure, not hard reps.
setup: Stand on one leg facing a mirror so you can see the knee and foot
Set the foot tripod and a level pelvis
Slowly bend and straighten the knee a few inches, continuously, for the whole interval
Keep the kneecap pointing over the 2nd/3rd toe the entire time
cues: Watch the knee in the mirror — keep it pointing at your middle toes, never diving inward
External-focus cue: 'spread the floor apart with your foot' and 'shine a headlight straight ahead with your kneecap'
Small, smooth, silent range — quality of the knee line is the whole drill
Easy effort, just grooving the pattern — this is a daily primer, not a hard set
